content: The O'nyong'nyong virus was first isolated in 1959 by the Uganda Virus Research Institute located in Entebbe, Uganda. This virus belongs to the Togaviridae family and is classified under the Alphavirus genus. It is closely related to the Chikungunya virus and the Igbo Ora virus. Transmission of the O'nyong'nyong virus occurs through the bite of an infected mosquito. Notably, it is the only known virus whose primary vectors are anopheline mosquitoes, specifically Anopheles funestus and Anopheles gambiae. Infection with the O'nyong'nyong virus typically presents with symptoms such as polyarthritis, rash, and fever. Additional symptoms may include eye pain, chest pain, lymphadenitis, and lethargy. Importantly, no fatalities have been reported as a result of infection with this virus. There have been two documented epidemics of O'nyong'nyong fever. The first epidemic occurred between 1959 and 1962, spreading from Uganda to Kenya, Tanzania, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Malawi, and Mozambique. This outbreak affected over two million individuals and is considered one of the largest arbovirus epidemics ever recorded. During this outbreak, the first isolates of the virus were obtained from mosquitoes and human blood samples collected in Gulu, northern Uganda, in 1959. The second epidemic took place in 1996–1997 and was confined to Uganda, affecting approximately 400 individuals. The 35-year gap between these two outbreaks, along with evidence of a potential outbreak in Uganda between 1904 and 1906, suggests that epidemics of the O'nyong'nyong virus may follow a cyclical pattern, occurring every 30 to 50 years.
